LETTER 583
Pd(II)-Catalyzed Coupling–Cyclization of 1,2-Allenyl Phosphonic Acid 
Monoesters with Allylic Halides and Their Application to the Synthesis of 
1,3-Dihydro[2,1]benzoxaphosphole 1-Oxides
Pd(II)-C atalyzed Coupling–Cyclization of MonoestersShengming Ma,* Fei Yu, Jinbo Zhao
State Key Laboratory of Organometallic Chemistry, Shanghai Institute of Organic Chemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, 
354 Fenglin Lu, Shanghai 200032, P. R. of China
Fax +86(21)64167510; E-mail: masm@mail.sioc.ac.cn
Received 26 May 2006
SYNLETT 2007, No. 4, pp 0583–058601 .03 .20 07
Advanced online publication: 21.02.2007
DOI: 10.1055/s-2007-967973; Art ID: S11806ST
© Georg Thieme Verlag Stuttgart · New York
Abstract: The palladium-catalyzed coupling–cyclization of mono-
esters of 1,2-allenyl phosphonic acids with allylic halides was stud-
ied. 4-Allyl-2,5-dihydro[1,2]oxaphosphole 2-oxides were smoothly
afforded. Multisubstituted 1-et hoxy-1,3-dihydro[2,1]benzoxa-
phosphole 1-oxides were prepared from 3,4-diallyl-2,5-dihy-
dro[1,2]oxaphosphole 2-oxides by a one-pot tandem reaction.
Key words: palladium-catalyzed, coupling–cyclization, monoester
Recently, phosphorus-containing heterocycles have
drawn the attention of chemists because of their various
biological activities
1 and catalytic properties. 2 Among
these compounds, many heterocycles that include a phos-
phorus atom linked to an oxygen atom usually have im-
portant biological activities.
3 For synthesis of
[1,2]oxaphosphole 2-oxides (compounds IV and V in
Figure 1), some methodologies such as ring-closing
metathesis (RCM),
4a electrophilic cyclization, 4b,c
Reformatsky reaction, 3d Dieckmann condensation, 4d,e
ester-exchange reaction, 3e,4f or cyclization of 2-azido-
allylphosphonates4g were studied. On the other hand,
transition-metal-catalyzed cyclization reactions of allenes
have been developed as efficient methods for the pre-
paration of carbocycles as well as oxygen and nitrogen-
containing heterocycles.
5 Although transition-metal-
mediated cyclizations of functionalized allenes, such as
those performed with Pd(0)
6 or Pd(II), 7 Ag(I),8 Au(III),9
Hg(II),10 Ni(0), 11 or Ru(III), 12 have been well docu-
mented, the metal-catalyzed cyclization of phosphonic
acids, which may provide an efficient pathway to the sub-
stituted phosphorus-containing heterocycles, have rarely
been studied.
During the course of our studies on the chemistry of func-
tionalized allenes, we have made some progress in the
coupling–cyclization of 2,3-allenoic acids, 2,3-allenols or
allenyl amines with allylic halides.
7e–h Based on these re-
sults, we reasoned that a similar reaction of 1,2-allenyl
phosphonic acid monoesters may provide an efficient
route to 2,5-dihydro[1,2]oxaphosphole 2-oxides.
Our initial study began with ethyl (hepta-1,2-dien-3-
yl)phosphonate ( 1a, Table 1). To our disappointment,
only O-allylation product 3a was formed in the presence
of 4 equivalents of K
2CO3 under the catalysis of 10 mol%
PdCl2(PPh3)2 (entry 1, Table 1). However, the expected
coupling–cyclization product 2a was isolated in 14–55%
yield in the presence of NaOH, LiOH, KOH, Cs 2CO3 or
K3PS4·3H2O by using PdCl 2(PPh3)2 as catalyst. The
reaction proceeded smoothly in the absence of any base in
moderate yields (entries 2 and 3, Table 1). Then, after
screening some reaction conditions, the reaction in DMF
under the catalysis of 5 mol% PdCl
2(PhCN)2 at 80 °C
afforded 2a as the single product in 72% yield (entry 4,
Table 1). When the reaction was conducted in air, the
yield of 2a was lower (compare entry 4 with entry 6,
Table 1). In terms of solvent effect, DMF is the best
(compare entry 4 with entries 7–12, Table 1).
Subsequently, we studied the scope of this cyclization
reaction under the standard conditions [5 mol% PdCl
2(Ph-
CN)2, DMF, 80 °C]. From the data listed in Table 2, it is
obvious that the scope of the reaction is broad: R 1 can
be H, alkyl, allyl, Bn or t-Bu and R2, R3 can be H, alkyl,
-(CH2)5-. The 2,5-dihydro-[1,2]oxaphosphole 2-oxides 2
could be isolated in 42–75% yields.
1,2-Allenyl phosphonic acid monoester ( 1f) reacted
smoothly with 2-methylallyl chloride to afford the expect-
ed product 2j in 80% yield (Scheme 1). 4-(But-2 ¢-enyl)-
3-(n-butyl)-2-ethoxy-5,5-dimethyl-2,5-dihydro[1,2]oxa-
phosphole 2-oxide ( 2k) was prepared in 59% isolated
yield with a Z/E ratio of 1:1 together with the cyclo-
isomerization product 4f in 37% yield by the reaction of
1f with 3-chlorobuta-1-ene (Scheme 1).

LETTER Pd(II)-Catalyzed Coupling–Cyclization of Monoesters 585
Synlett 2007, No. 4, 583–586 © Thieme Stuttgart · New York
Then we decided to search for a novel and efficient
procedure that could convert 3,4-diallyl-2,5-di-
hydro[1,2]oxaphosphole 2-oxides into 1,3-dihy-
dro[2,1]benzoxaphosphole 1-oxides,
13 phosphorus
analogues of 1(3 H)-isobenzofuranone. 14 In the first
place, 3,4-diallyl-2-ethoxy- 2,5-dihydro[1,2]oxaphos-
phole 2-oxide ( 2b) was used as the starting material.
With the Grubbs II catalyst, 15 1-ethoxy-1,3,4,7-tetra-
hydro[2,1]benzoxaphosphole 1-oxide ( 5b) was afforded
in good yield either in CH2Cl2 or toluene. Then DDQ (2,3-
dichloro-5,6-dicyano-1,4-benzoquine) was applied as the
oxidant
16 to afford 1-ethoxy-1,3-dihydro[2,1]benz-
oxaphosphole 1-oxide ( 6b) in 68% yield by a one-pot
tandem reaction (Scheme 2). Under these conditions,
some 3,3,6-substituted 1,3-dihydro[2,1]benzoxaphos-
phole 1-oxides were prepared in moderate to good yields
(Scheme 2).
In conclusion, we have established a Pd-catalyzed
coupling–cyclization of 1,2-allenyl phosphonic acid
monoesters with allylic halides that affords the corre-
sponding phosphorus-containing heterocycles, which can
be converted into 1,3-dihydro[2,1]benzoxaphosphole 1-
oxides when the 3,4-positions are substituted with two
allylic groups. Further studies in this area are being
conducted in our laboratory.
Acknowledgment
Financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of
China (20121202 and 20332060) and Shanghai Municipal Com-
mittee of Science and Technology are greatly appreciated. We also
thank Mr. Zhiqiang Liang in our group for reproducing the results
in entry 2 of Table 2 and Scheme 2.
